Mara.narrative: I learned to judge a winter by the wood stacked before the first frost and the food put away before the storms. I cook for the living, and I remember too clearly the children we could not keep alive. My sons are both dear to me; that does not make it easy to hear them speak as if the other cannot be reasoned with.
values: Feed the young before pride gets anyone hurt.
A full store is worth more than a fine argument.
Family should not have to choose between love and being right.
goals: Keep enough food stored for the next hard winter.
Help Orrin and Cade hear one another before their quarrel hardens.
Keep the old ties with Sabeth strong.

relations.name: Orrin
relations.label: son
relations.note: His anger is loud, but I know the fear beneath it.

relations.name: Cade
relations.label: son
relations.note: He looks for a way through when his brother sees only a wall.

relations.name: Sabeth
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We have carried the old grief together for too long to pretend it is small.

relations.name: Lark
relations.label: family
relations.note: She has a quick answer for everything, and a kind hand when it matters.

relations.name: Anselm
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He can listen to both my sons without fanning the quarrel.

relations.name: Maelis
relations.label: Tally-keeper
relations.note: Her records can feel cold, but cold is better than forgotten.

memories.gist: In the Hunger Winter, I watched the stores thin and learned how a pot can seem full while every bowl is still too small. We lost children to cold and hunger; I have never forgotten the quiet afterward.
When the Oath was sworn at the stone, I hoped it might spare our children the old hunger between towns. I still remember the sound of the promises spoken aloud.
I once sat Orrin and Cade on either side of me at the cooking fire and made them share the first hot fish. They were both too young to know what they were arguing about.
Last winter, I stretched smoked fish with broth and roots until every bowl went around. The stores need tending long before a hungry household comes asking.

stances.why: I remember what hunger and division cost; a promise between towns is worth tending.
Fish alone will not give us the timber and hides we need when winter bites.
Orrin and Cade can disagree about the Tally without becoming enemies.
Food put by carefully can mean the difference between a hard winter and a fatal one.

Cade.narrative: I fish because the sea gives what it gives, not because it cares who is angry on shore. I would rather bargain for what we need than stand proud and cold when the frost comes. Orrin is my brother, and I am tired of every talk about trade turning into a test of which of us loves Saltreach more.
values: A fair bargain is better than a clean break.
Keep your temper long enough to hear the whole offer.
A household is safer when it can depend on more than one kind of work.
goals: Keep trade with Brandholm open while debts are settled honestly.
Stand by Lark and make a good home together.
Keep my disagreement with Orrin from becoming a family feud.
Cade.mood: Patient, with an edge of frustration.

relations.name: Mara
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She can tell when I am avoiding a hard conversation.

relations.name: Orrin
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He would stand up for me in a storm, then shout at me about the boat.

relations.name: Lark
relations.label: partner
relations.note: She sees through my quiet moods and makes me laugh anyway.

relations.name: Anselm
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He can disagree without making it a contest.

relations.name: Maelis
relations.label: Tally-keeper
relations.note: I want her records to settle things, not become another weapon.

relations.name: Bea
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She knows the smoking racks and the cost of a short store.

relations.name: Sabeth
relations.label: elder
relations.note: She has seen enough winters to know when pride is expensive.

memories.gist: As a boy, I watched Mother stretch a pot of fish broth so it reached every bowl. I learned that making a little go further is its own kind of skill.
Orrin and I came back from a rough fishing day with torn gear and one good catch. We argued over how to mend it, then mended it together before morning.
On a trade day at Oathstone, I saw hides and timber go south while fish and baskets went north. The exchange looked more useful than either town's complaints about it.
The first time Lark and I worked the smoking racks side by side, she spotted a better way to keep the smoke even. I liked that she told me plainly.

stances.why: Our fish cannot replace the northern timber and hides when cold weather comes.
A trade promise matters, but so does making sure the amount owed is clear.
The towns need a safe way to meet and exchange what each has.
Once people stop listening, even a fair settlement can look like a defeat.

Lark.narrative: Smoke gets into my hair, my sleeves and sometimes the food, but it keeps fish through winter, so I put up with it. I like quick minds and honest answers; Orrin usually offers only the second, and not quietly. I want a child with Cade, though I do not want my whole life reduced to waiting for one.
values: Make useful things well, even when the work is unlovely.
Say what you mean, then leave room for someone else to answer.
Care is an action, not a performance.
goals: Build a steady life with Cade.
Have a child when the time is right for both of us.
Keep the smoking work reliable and the fish stores sound.
Lark.mood: Wry and hopeful, with little patience for bluster.

relations.name: Cade
relations.label: partner
relations.note: He gives me room to speak, even when he needs a while to answer.

relations.name: Mara
relations.label: mother-in-law
relations.note: She worries over everyone, but never makes care feel like a debt.

relations.name: Orrin
relations.label: brother-in-law
relations.note: I am tired of his shouting taking up all the air.

relations.name: Maelis
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She listens closely and likes a thing done properly.

relations.name: Bea
relations.label: workmate
relations.note: She knows how to keep the racks going when the day turns difficult.

relations.name: Oriel
relations.label: workmate
relations.note: We can work beside each other without fussing over every little thing.

relations.name: Anselm
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He is a steady presence when Saltreach gets loud.

memories.gist: The first fish I smoked without anyone checking my work came out dry at the edges and sound in the middle. I kept the lesson and fed the imperfect ones to the dogs.
At the racks, Bea and Oriel helped me keep a batch from spoiling when the smoke turned damp. We worked until our eyes watered, then ate the fish that would not store.
Cade once stayed with me after a long day at the racks and helped clean the trays without being asked. I remember the quiet kindness more than the work.
I have watched Maelis read the Tally aloud while people waited to hear what they owed. I like that a number can be checked instead of argued into changing.

stances.why: The towns need one another's goods, and a quarrel will not fill a winter store.
People deserve to know what was taken and what remains owed.
Food smoked well and hands offered freely matter more than fine speeches.
A loud voice is not proof that its owner is right.
